absolute-reference.short: A spreadsheet address with $ signs, such as $E$1, that stays the same when a formula is copied to other cells.

array.short: An ordered list or table of numbers; a linear program's costs c, rule table A and limits b are arrays.

assert.short: A line of code that stops a program with a message when a stated condition is false.

agc.short: The grid operator's computer system that raises or lowers plants over minutes to bring frequency back to 60 Hz.

average-power.short: The energy used over a period divided by the length of that period.

balancing.short: Keeping the power that plants make equal to the power that people use, at every moment.

balancing-authority.short: The organisation that keeps supply and demand balanced, moment to moment, in its own part of the grid.

battery-duration.short: How many hours a battery can discharge at its rated power: its energy in MWh divided by its power in MW.

forecast-bias.short: The average signed miss of a forecast, showing whether it tends to run too high or too low.

binding-constraint.short: A rule that holds exactly at the selected plan, with no room to spare; loosening it may or may not improve the best cost.

bus.short: A point of the network where plants, loads and lines meet, such as a substation; a network model has one balance rule per bus.

capacity.short: The most power a plant can produce at once, often called its nameplate size.

capacity-expansion.short: An optimization model that decides what to build, as well as how to run it, at least cost.

capacity-factor.short: The energy a plant actually made over a period, divided by the energy it would have made running at full capacity the whole time.

capital-cost.short: The money spent to build a power plant, usually given per kilowatt of capacity, before it makes any electricity.

capital-recovery-factor.short: The share of a building cost that must be repaid each year, with interest, to pay it off over a given number of years.

carbon-intensity.short: The CO2 emitted for each unit of electricity, for example in tonnes per megawatt-hour.

carbon-price.short: A charge per tonne of CO2 emitted, added to costs so that cleaner choices become relatively cheaper.

clearing-price.short: The price at which supply meets demand in a market, paid to every seller that runs in that hour.

combined-cycle.short: A gas power plant that burns gas in a turbine and uses the hot exhaust to make steam for a second turbine, so it gets more electricity from the same fuel.

congestion.short: A power line carrying all it is allowed to, so cheaper power cannot reach where it is needed and prices can differ by location.

congestion-rent.short: What loads pay at their locational prices minus what generators are paid at theirs; in a DC model it equals the sum, over the full lines, of each line's shadow price times its flow.

constraint.short: A rule every solution must obey, such as supply equals demand or no plant above its size.

utc.short: The world reference clock, with no daylight saving; EIA stamps its hourly grid data in it.

counterfactual.short: What would have happened without the change being judged; every saving or effect is measured against one.

cube-law.short: The power carried by the wind grows with the cube of its speed (twice the speed, eight times the power); a turbine's output follows it only between its cut-in and rated speeds.

curtailment.short: Turning a wind or solar farm below what the weather allows, usually because the grid has more power than it can use at that moment.

cut-in-speed.short: The lowest wind speed at which a turbine starts to make electricity.

cut-out-speed.short: The wind speed above which a turbine shuts down to protect itself.

dataframe.short: A pandas table with named columns and an index, such as one row per hour.

day-ahead-forecast.short: A grid operator's estimate, made the day before, of how much power customers will use in each hour.

daylight-saving-time.short: Clocks moved an hour ahead in summer, giving one 23-hour day in spring and one 25-hour day in autumn.

dc-power-flow.short: A linear approximation of real-power flows that sets each line's flow from the voltage-angle difference across it, holds voltage magnitudes fixed, assumes small angles, and leaves out losses and reactive power.

decision-variable.short: A quantity the model is free to choose, such as how much each plant makes each hour.

demand.short: The total power that all users on a grid draw at a given moment.

demand-response.short: Electricity users cutting or shifting their use when the grid asks, usually in return for a payment.

discount-rate.short: The yearly rate used to turn money paid or received in the future into its value today.

dispatch.short: Deciding how much power each plant should make, hour by hour or minute by minute.

dispatchable.short: A power plant whose output the operator can turn up or down on request, such as a gas plant.

dominated-plan.short: A plan that another plan beats on every count: no more cost, no more emissions, and better on at least one.

duck-curve.short: The daily shape of demand minus solar output, with a dip at midday and a steep climb in the evening.

duration-curve.short: A year of hourly values sorted from highest to lowest, showing for how many hours each level is reached.

electrification.short: Switching a use of energy, such as heating or driving, from burning fuel to using electricity.

emissions-cap.short: A limit on the total CO2 that may be emitted in a period, such as a year.

energy.short: An amount of electricity made or used over a stretch of time, equal to power multiplied by time and measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh) or megawatt-hours (MWh).

energy-burden.short: The share of a household's income spent on energy bills.

energy-security.short: Keeping energy flowing at bearable prices when a fuel, a supplier or a route is cut off.

energy-storage.short: Equipment, such as a battery, that takes in electricity at one time and gives it back later, with some losses.

epsilon-constraint.short: A way to trace a trade-off by optimizing one goal while capping the other, then moving the cap step by step.

evidence-ladder.short: The stages a project climbs: announced, funded, permitted, under construction, operating and at design output.

fast-frequency-response.short: Power from batteries or other inverter-based resources delivered within a fraction of a second of a frequency drop.

feasible-region.short: The set of all plans that meet every rule of a model; on a two-variable chart it is a shaded polygon.

fermi-estimate.short: A quick estimate built from round numbers and a few simple steps, aiming to get the order of magnitude right.

firm-capacity.short: Power that can be counted on whenever it is needed, whatever the weather.

firm-share.short: The part of a plant's capacity that a grid counts on in its riskiest hours, often estimated as its effective load-carrying capability (ELCC) and set per technology class.

fixed-charge.short: A part of a power bill that is the same each month however much electricity the home uses.

fixed-om.short: Operation and maintenance costs a plant pays every year whether or not it runs, such as staff and insurance.

flexibility.short: The ability of a plant, a store or a group of users to raise or lower power quickly when the grid asks.

forecast-error.short: The difference between what was forecast, such as tomorrow's demand or wind, and what actually happened.

frozen-telemetry.short: A measurement feed stuck on its last value, which shows up as the same reading hour after hour.

gigawatt.short: A thousand megawatts, a rate of energy flow used for large plants, whole fleets and national demand.

governor.short: A plant's speed control that opens or closes its steam, gas or water valves as the grid frequency changes.

frequency.short: The number of cycles per second of the grid's alternating current, 60 hertz (Hz) in North America, which falls when power is short and rises when there is too much.

heat-pump.short: A device that uses electricity to move heat, into a building to warm it or out of it to cool it.

heat-rate.short: The fuel energy a power plant burns to make one megawatt-hour, for example in MMBtu per MWh, so lower means more efficient.

hour-ending.short: A time stamp that labels each hour by its last moment, so 01:00 means the hour from midnight to 01:00.

inequality.short: A rule that allows a range of values, written with ≤ (at most) or ≥ (at least).

inertia.short: Energy stored in the spinning machines of a power grid; it slows a fall in frequency but cannot stop it.

infeasible.short: Said of a model whose rules contradict each other, so that no plan meets them all.

inverter.short: Power electronics that convert the direct current of solar panels and batteries, or a wind turbine's varying output, into the grid's alternating current.

kilowatt.short: A unit of power equal to 1,000 watts.

kilowatt-hour.short: The unit of energy on a household electricity bill: one kilowatt kept up for one hour.

lcoe.short: A plant's lifetime costs divided by the electricity it makes over its life, both discounted to today's money, giving an average cost per megawatt-hour.

linear-program.short: An optimization problem in which the goal and all the rules are linear, so each is a sum of quantities times fixed numbers.

load-factor.short: Average demand over a period divided by the peak demand in that period.

load-relief.short: The small drop in demand when the frequency falls, because many motors turn a little slower and draw less power.

load-duration-curve.short: A year's hourly demand sorted from highest to lowest, showing for how many hours each level of demand is needed.

locational-marginal-price.short: The extra cost per megawatt-hour of serving a small increase in demand at one place on the grid in one interval, given the plants running and the limits of the lines.

log-scale.short: A scale on which each equal step multiplies the value by the same factor, often 10, so tiny and huge values fit on one chart.

marginal-cost.short: What one more unit costs, here the extra running cost of one more megawatt-hour of demand.

marginal-plant.short: The plant that serves the last megawatt of demand, whose offer sets the clearing price.

mae.short: The average size of a forecast's misses, in the units of what is forecast, ignoring whether they were too high or too low.

mape.short: The average miss as a percentage of the actual value; it breaks down when actual values are near zero.

median.short: The middle value of a set sorted from lowest to highest: half the values lie below it, half above.

megawatt.short: A unit of power equal to one million watts, or a thousand kilowatts.

megawatt-hour.short: A unit of energy: one megawatt kept up for one hour, or a thousand kilowatt-hours.

merit-order.short: Running power plants in order of their running cost, cheapest first.

mixed-integer-program.short: An optimization model in which some decisions must be whole numbers, such as a plant being on (1) or off (0).

mmbtu.short: One million British thermal units, a unit of fuel heat; about 0.29 MWh of heat, and gas is priced in dollars per MMBtu.

multi-objective.short: A choice with several goals that cannot all be at their best at once.

nadir.short: The lowest point the frequency reaches after a power plant trips, before it starts to recover.

negative-price.short: A wholesale price below zero, which happens when the last plant needed would rather pay than stop running.

net-demand.short: Demand minus the output of wind and solar, which is what the other power plants must still supply.

objective.short: What an optimization tries to make as small or as large as possible, such as the total cost.

operating-emissions.short: The CO2 released where fuel is burned to make electricity, leaving out building the plant and producing and delivering its fuel.

optimality-gap.short: For a mixed-integer program, the remaining distance between the best plan the solver has found and the bound it has proven, so 0% means proven best.

optimization.short: Finding the best choice among many, given a goal and the rules the choice must obey.

overnight-cost.short: The cost to build a power plant as if it were built overnight, so with no interest paid during construction, usually given per kilowatt.

parameter.short: A number a model is given and takes as it is, such as demand or a plant's running cost, as opposed to a decision it makes.

pareto-frontier.short: The set of plans that cannot be made cheaper without becoming dirtier, or cleaner without becoming more expensive.

peak-demand.short: The highest demand in a period, such as the busiest hour of a year; the grid must be able to meet it, with a margin.

peaker.short: A power plant that runs only in the hours of highest demand, because it starts quickly but is expensive to run.

persistence-forecast.short: The simplest forecast: the next value will be the same as the last one seen, or as the same hour a day or a week before.

power.short: How fast electricity is being made or used at a given moment, measured in watts, kilowatts (kW) or megawatts (MW).

power-coefficient.short: The share of the wind's power that a turbine turns into electricity; no rotor can capture more than 16/27, about 59% (the Betz limit).

power-curve.short: A chart of how much power a wind turbine makes at each wind speed.

prediction-interval.short: A range that should contain the actual value with a stated probability, drawn as a band around a forecast.

present-value.short: What an amount of money paid or received in the future is worth today, once it is discounted.

primary-response.short: Automatic extra output from power plants' governors within seconds of a frequency drop; it stops the fall but does not restore 60 Hz.

production-credit.short: A payment for each megawatt-hour a plant produces, set by a policy such as a tax credit.

projection.short: A model's estimate of a future quantity under stated assumptions, not a measurement or a promise.

quartile.short: The values that cut a sorted set into four equal parts: 25% of values lie below the first, 50% below the second (the median), 75% below the third.

ramp-rate.short: How fast a power plant can raise or lower its output, for example in megawatts per minute or per hour.

rocof.short: How fast the grid's frequency moves in the first instant after a disturbance, in hertz per second.

rated-speed.short: The wind speed at which a turbine first reaches its full rated power; above it, the blades turn to spill the extra wind.

reactance.short: A line's opposition to alternating current; when several paths join two places, each carries a share of the power that falls as its reactance rises.

reactive-power.short: The part of alternating-current power that does no net work but holds voltage up; it is supplied and absorbed locally.

refuelling-outage.short: The planned weeks when a reactor is shut down to replace part of its fuel and carry out maintenance.

representative-period.short: A real stretch of time, such as a week, chosen to stand for many similar ones so that a model can run faster.

resample.short: Regroup a time series to a coarser step, such as hours to days, by averaging or summing.

reserve-margin.short: The capacity counted as available at the peak, above the year's peak demand, as a percentage of that peak.

reserves.short: Spare capacity that operators keep ready to cover the sudden loss of a plant or a forecast that misses.

round-trip-efficiency.short: The share of the energy put into storage that comes back out.

running-cost.short: What it costs a plant to make one more megawatt-hour, mostly fuel, leaving out the cost of building it.

sensitivity-analysis.short: Changing a model's inputs one at a time and re-solving, to see which inputs the answer depends on.

shadow-price.short: How much the best total cost would change if one rule were loosened by one unit; for the rule that supply equals demand, it is the price of one more megawatt-hour.

simplex-method.short: A way to solve linear programs by moving from corner to neighbouring corner of the feasible region, never making the goal worse, until no neighbour is better.

skill-score.short: How much smaller a forecast's error is than that of a simple baseline such as persistence.

solver.short: Software that finds the best solution of an optimization problem, or shows that none exists.

standard-deviation.short: A measure of spread: roughly, how far a typical value lies from the mean.

state-of-charge.short: The energy a battery holds at a given moment, in MWh; it links each hour of a storage schedule to the next.

supply-diversity.short: How evenly the energy supply is spread over different sources, so that losing one does not lose most of it.

supply-stack.short: All the offers to sell power in one hour, lined up from the cheapest to the most expensive.

system-boundary.short: The line that decides which parts, costs and emissions a study counts and which it leaves out.

telemetry.short: Measurements sent automatically from plants and substations to the grid operator.

terawatt-hour.short: A unit of energy equal to a billion kilowatt-hours, used for the yearly electricity use of regions and countries.

tornado-chart.short: A chart that ranks inputs by how far a result moves when each input is swung from a low to a high value, one at a time.

unbounded.short: Said of a model whose goal can improve without limit, which usually means a rule is missing.

ufls.short: Relays that automatically disconnect blocks of customers when the frequency falls to a set level, to save the rest of the grid.

unit-commitment.short: Deciding which plants are on in each hour, before deciding how much each one produces.

unserved-energy.short: Demand that could not be met, so some customers lost power.

validation.short: Checking that a model represents the real system well enough for the question it is used to answer.

variable-om.short: Operation and maintenance costs, apart from fuel, that grow with every megawatt-hour a plant makes.

variable-renewables.short: Wind and solar power, whose output follows the weather: they can be turned down but not up.

verification.short: Checking that a model does what its equations say, with tests such as units, the energy balance and hand-solved cases.

voltage.short: The electrical pressure that pushes current along a line; grids hold it within a narrow band at every point.

watt-hour.short: A unit of energy: one watt kept up for one hour; 1,000 Wh make one kilowatt-hour.

wacc.short: The blended return a project must pay its lenders and its owners, used as the project's discount rate.

weighted-sum.short: A way to combine several goals into one score by adding them up, each multiplied by a weight.

wholesale-price.short: The price at which electricity is traded between power plants and the companies that sell it to customers, often set hour by hour.
